decks.title: Principles of Inheritance — Part 1: Mendel’s laws
goals: Use the terms of genetics correctly
State Mendel’s principles and the reasons for his success
Work out monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, back crosses and test crosses with Punnett squares

slides.heading: Principles of Inheritance
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how characters pass from parents to offspring, as Mendel first worked out.

visual.alt: Flow showing heredity and variation as the subject of genetics

slides.narration: Children resemble their parents, yet no two siblings are exactly alike. Heredity is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring, and variation is the degree to which offspring differ. Genetics studies both. Gregor Mendel, working with garden peas from 1856 to 1863, discovered the basic rules.

slides.heading: Terms of genetics
slides.body_md: A clear vocabulary makes crosses easy to describe.

rows: Unit of inheritance that controls a character
Alternative forms of a gene, e.g. T (tall) and t (dwarf)
A pair of chromosomes with the same genes in the same positions
Chromosomes not involved in sex determination, and those that are (X, Y)
Genetic make-up, e.g. TT, Tt, tt
Two identical alleles (TT, tt) / two different alleles (Tt)

visual.alt: Table of genetic terms and their meanings

slides.narration: Each character is controlled by a gene that comes in alternative forms called alleles. An organism carries two alleles for each gene, one on each of a pair of homologous chromosomes. Its genotype is the pair of alleles; its phenotype is what we see.

slides.heading: Why Mendel succeeded
slides.body_md: Mendel chose the **garden pea** and worked carefully.

rows: Easy to grow, short life cycle, naturally self-pollinating with true-breeding lines, and easy to cross artificially
Clear either/or traits such as tall/dwarf, round/wrinkled seeds
One or two characters at a time
Ratios became reliable; records kept carefully
The characters he chose were on different chromosomes or far apart, so they assorted independently

visual.alt: Table of reasons for Mendel’s success

slides.narration: Mendel used true-breeding lines, counted thousands of plants and applied mathematics to biology for the first time. He also studied traits one or two at a time, which revealed simple ratios that earlier workers had missed.

slides.heading: Monohybrid cross
slides.body_md: Crossing true-breeding tall (TT) with dwarf (tt) gives an all-tall **F1 (Tt)**. Selfing the F1 gives an **F2** in which tall : dwarf = **3 : 1**, and genotypes TT : Tt : tt = **1 : 2 : 1**.

slides.narration: The dwarf character disappears in the first generation and reappears in a quarter of the second. Mendel concluded that factors come in pairs, that one can be dominant over the other, and that the pair separates when gametes form.

slides.heading: Mendel’s first two laws
slides.body_md: From monohybrid crosses Mendel proposed:

rows: Characters are controlled by discrete factors that occur in pairs; in a dissimilar pair one (dominant) expresses itself over the other (recessive)
The two alleles of a pair do not blend; they separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one allele

visual.alt: Table of the laws of dominance and segregation

slides.narration: The law of dominance explains why the first hybrid generation shows only one parental form and why the second generation shows a three-to-one ratio. The law of segregation, sometimes called the law of purity of gametes, explains why the recessive form reappears unchanged.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: the test cross
slides.body_md: A tall pea plant may be TT or Tt. How can its genotype be found? Predict the ratios.
bullets: Cross it with a **homozygous recessive** dwarf (tt): a **test cross**.
If it is TT, all offspring are tall (Tt).
If it is Tt, tall : dwarf $= 1 : 1$ (computed from Tt $\times$ tt).
A cross of the F1 with either parent is a **back cross**; the test cross is the back cross with the recessive parent.

visual.alt: Worked table: test-cross ratios all tall or 1 : 1

slides.narration: A recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, so the offspring reveal exactly what the unknown parent passed on. If any dwarf offspring appear, the tall parent must have carried a hidden dwarf allele.

slides.heading: Quick check: test cross
slides.body_md: What ratio is expected when a heterozygous tall plant is test-crossed?
slides.narration: Quick check. Half the gametes carry the recessive allele.

slides.narration: Sixteen combinations of gametes give four kinds of seed. Round yellow and wrinkled green are the parental types; round green and wrinkled yellow are new combinations, which could appear only if the two genes are inherited independently.

slides.heading: Law of independent assortment
slides.body_md: When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is **independent** of the other pair. Each F1 forms **four kinds of gametes** (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal proportions.

visual.alt: Table showing the dihybrid ratio as a product of two monohybrid ratios

slides.narration: Each gene on its own still gives three to one, so the dihybrid ratio is simply the product of two monohybrid ratios. This works only because the genes are on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting numbers
slides.body_md: An F2 from RrYy × RrYy has 1600 seeds. How many of each phenotype are expected?
bullets: Round yellow $= \dfrac{9}{16} \times 1600 = 900$; round green $= \dfrac{3}{16} \times 1600 = 300$.
Wrinkled yellow $= \dfrac{3}{16} \times 1600 = 300$; wrinkled green $= \dfrac{1}{16} \times 1600 = 100$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 900, 300, 300, 100 seeds

slides.narration: Multiply each fraction by the total. Nine sixteenths of sixteen hundred is nine hundred; three sixteenths is three hundred; one sixteenth is one hundred. Real counts will be close to these but rarely exact.

slides.body_md: How many kinds of gametes does an RrYy plant form?
slides.narration: Quick check. Combine one allele of each gene.

slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about Mendel’s results.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Terms: gene, allele, homologous chromosomes, autosomes, sex chromosomes, genotype, phenotype, homozygous, heterozygous.
Mendel’s success: pea, true-breeding lines, seven contrasting pairs, one or two traits at a time, large samples, statistics.
Monohybrid F2: 3 : 1 phenotypes, 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes; laws of dominance and segregation.
Test cross with recessive parent: all dominant (homozygous) or 1 : 1 (heterozygous); back cross with either parent.
Dihybrid F2: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; law of independent assortment.

visual.alt: Summary table of three key ratios

slides.narration: To recap: Mendel’s careful experiments with peas revealed that factors come in pairs, separate into gametes and, for different characters, assort independently. The three-to-one, one-to-one and nine-three-three-one ratios follow from these rules.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always write **gametes** before the Punnett square.
Give **both** phenotypic and genotypic ratios for monohybrid crosses.
Distinguish **test cross** from **back cross**.
State each law in Mendel’s own sense, not just its name.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Show the gametes before drawing the square. Give both kinds of ratio. Keep test cross and back cross apart. And state each law fully.

goals: Explain incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple alleles
Explain polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy with examples
Explain the chromosomal theory of inheritance, linkage and crossing over

slides.heading: Deviations from Mendelism
slides.body_md: Part 2 — cases that Mendel’s simple rules do not fully describe.

visual.alt: Flow of five deviations from simple Mendelian inheritance

slides.narration: Mendel’s laws still hold: alleles segregate and assort. But dominance is not always complete, a gene may have more than two alleles, a character may depend on many genes, and one gene may affect many characters.

slides.heading: Incomplete dominance: snapdragon
slides.body_md: In the snapdragon (dog flower), a cross between true-breeding **red (RR)** and **white (rr)** gives **pink (Rr)** F1 plants. The F2 shows red : pink : white = **1 : 2 : 1**, so the **phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio**.

slides.narration: Neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote has an intermediate colour. The alleles have not blended, though: red and white reappear unchanged in the next generation.

slides.heading: Codominance and multiple alleles: ABO blood groups
slides.body_md: The ABO blood group is controlled by gene **I** with three alleles, **Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i**. Iᴬ and Iᴮ produce slightly different sugars on red cells; i produces none. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are **codominant** (both expressed in Iᴬ Iᴮ), and both are dominant over i. A person carries only two of the three alleles.

visual.alt: Table of ABO genotypes and blood groups

slides.narration: Three alleles give six genotypes but only four blood groups. Group AB shows codominance: both sugars appear. Because there are more than two alleles in the population, ABO is also an example of multiple alleles.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: blood groups of children
slides.body_md: A mother of group A (Iᴬi) and a father of group B (Iᴮi) have children. Which blood groups are possible, and in what proportion?
bullets: Gametes: mother Iᴬ or i; father Iᴮ or i.
Children: Iᴬ Iᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O), each with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$.
So all **four** groups are possible, in the ratio **1 : 1 : 1 : 1**.

visual.alt: Worked table: each blood group with probability one quarter

slides.narration: Two heterozygous parents of groups A and B can have a child of any of the four groups. This is why blood groups alone can only exclude, never prove, parentage.

slides.heading: Quick check: blood groups
slides.body_md: Which genotype gives blood group O?
slides.narration: Quick check. It has no Iᴬ or Iᴮ allele.

slides.heading: Polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy
slides.body_md: **Polygenic inheritance:** a character controlled by **several genes** with additive effects, giving continuous variation, e.g. **human skin colour** (three genes A, B, C) and height. **Pleiotropy:** **one gene** with **multiple phenotypic effects**.

rows: A mutation in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase causes mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation
Gene B: BB makes much starch (large grains, round seeds); bb little (small grains, wrinkled seeds); Bb round seeds but intermediate grain size — so dominance depends on the phenotype considered

visual.alt: Table of two examples of pleiotropy

slides.narration: Skin colour shows many shades because each dominant allele adds a little pigment. Pleiotropy is the opposite situation: one gene, many effects. In peas the same starch gene controls both seed shape and starch grain size, and the heterozygote is dominant for one but intermediate for the other.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: polygenic classes
slides.body_md: Skin colour is controlled by three additive genes. A man and a woman are both AaBbCc. How many phenotype classes can their children show, and what fraction is expected to be as dark as AABBCC?
bullets: Number of dominant alleles can be 0 to 6, so classes $= 2k + 1 = 2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$.
Darkest (AABBCC) $= \left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{64} \approx 0.0156$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 7 classes, 1/64 darkest

slides.narration: Each child can carry anywhere from zero to six dominant alleles, giving seven shades. The chance of getting the dominant allele for all three genes from both parents is one quarter cubed, one in sixty-four.

slides.heading: Pedigree analysis
slides.body_md: In humans, controlled crosses are not possible, so the inheritance of a trait is studied in a family tree, a **pedigree**, using standard symbols.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: recombination frequency
slides.body_md: In a test cross of a dihybrid fruit fly, 1000 offspring include 880 parental types and 120 recombinants. Find the recombination frequency and comment on the linkage.
bullets: Recombination frequency $= \dfrac{120}{1000} \times 100 = 12$ percent.
This is far below the 50 percent expected for unlinked genes, so the genes are **linked**, fairly close together on one chromosome.

visual.alt: Worked table: recombination frequency 12 percent

slides.narration: Unlinked genes would give equal parental and recombinant types, fifty percent each. Only twelve percent recombinants means the genes usually travel together, so they are linked; the low value shows they lie quite close.

bullets: Incomplete dominance: snapdragon, F2 1 : 2 : 1 (phenotype = genotype).
Codominance and multiple alleles: ABO (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i); AB codominant; six genotypes, four groups.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In incomplete dominance, say the alleles **do not blend** — parental types reappear.
Write ABO genotypes with **Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i**.
Give a **reason** when identifying a pedigree pattern.
Use **recombination frequency** to judge distance between genes.

notes.title: Principles of Inheritance — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Heredity, variation and the terms of genetics
sections.body_md:
**Heredity** is the transmission of characters from parents to offspring; **variation** is the degree by which progeny differ from their parents and from each other. **Genetics** deals with both.

- **Gene (Mendel’s factor):** the unit of inheritance controlling a character.
- **Alleles:** alternative forms of a gene (e.g. T for tall and t for dwarf).
- **Homologous chromosomes:** a pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the same genes at the same positions (loci).
- **Autosomes** are chromosomes not concerned with sex determination; **sex chromosomes** (X and Y in humans) determine sex.
- **Genotype:** genetic constitution (TT, Tt, tt). **Phenotype:** observable expression (tall, dwarf).
- **Homozygous:** two identical alleles (TT or tt); **heterozygous:** two different alleles (Tt).
- **Dominant** allele expresses itself in the heterozygote; **recessive** allele expresses only when homozygous.

**Mendel’s work.** Gregor Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas (*Pisum sativum*) for seven years (1856–1863) and proposed the laws of inheritance. He selected **seven pairs of contrasting characters**: stem height (tall/dwarf), flower colour (violet/white), flower position (axial/terminal), pod shape (inflated/constricted), pod colour (green/yellow), seed shape (round/wrinkled) and seed colour (yellow/green).

**Reasons for Mendel’s success:** pea is easy to grow, has a short life cycle, is naturally self-pollinating (giving **true-breeding lines**) and is easy to cross-pollinate artificially; he chose clear contrasting characters; studied **one or two characters at a time**; used **large samples** and applied **statistics**; kept careful records; and the characters he chose happened to assort independently.

key_terms.definition_md: An alternative form of a gene.
The genetic constitution of an organism.
The observable expression of a character.
A line that, on continuous self-pollination, shows stable inheritance of a character for several generations.

visual.alt: Table of Mendel’s seven pairs of contrasting characters

sections.heading: 2. Monohybrid and dihybrid crosses
sections.body_md:
**Monohybrid cross.** True-breeding tall (TT) × dwarf (tt) → F1 all tall (Tt). F1 selfed → F2: **3 tall : 1 dwarf** (phenotypic ratio) and **1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt** (genotypic ratio). The **Punnett square**, devised by Reginald Punnett, shows all possible gamete combinations.

**Law of dominance:** characters are controlled by discrete units called factors, which occur in pairs; in a dissimilar pair one member (dominant) dominates the other (recessive). It explains the expression of only one parental character in the F1 and both in the F2.

**Law of segregation:** the alleles do not show any blending, and both characters are recovered as such in the F2; the two alleles of a pair **segregate** during gamete formation so that each gamete receives only one (law of purity of gametes).

**Back cross and test cross.** A **back cross** is a cross of the F1 with either parent. A **test cross** is a cross of an organism showing the dominant phenotype with the **recessive parent** to find its genotype: Tt × tt gives **1 dominant : 1 recessive**; TT × tt gives all dominant.

**Dihybrid cross.** Round yellow (RRYY) × wrinkled green (rryy) → F1 all round yellow (RrYy). F1 selfed → F2: **9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green**. Each gene alone still segregates 3 : 1.

**Law of independent assortment:** when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair. The F1 forms four kinds of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) in equal frequency, so (3 : 1) × (3 : 1) = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

key_terms.definition_md: A cross involving one pair of contrasting characters.
A cross of a dominant-phenotype individual with a homozygous recessive to find its genotype.
A cross of the F1 hybrid with either parent.
Alleles of different genes segregate independently during gamete formation.

sections.heading: 3. Deviations from Mendelism: incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple alleles
sections.body_md:
**Incomplete dominance.** In **snapdragon** (*Antirrhinum*, dog flower), true-breeding red (RR) × white (rr) gives **pink (Rr)** F1. F2: red : pink : white = **1 : 2 : 1**, the same as the genotypic ratio. The heterozygote is intermediate because neither allele is completely dominant; the alleles do not blend, since red and white reappear.

**Codominance.** Both alleles of a heterozygote are fully expressed. **ABO blood groups** are controlled by gene **I** with three alleles: **Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i**. Iᴬ and Iᴮ produce slightly different forms of a sugar polymer on the surface of red blood cells; i produces none. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are completely dominant over i, but when both are present (IᴬIᴮ) both are expressed: **codominance**, giving group **AB**.

**Multiple alleles.** More than two alleles govern the same character in a population (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i), though any one person carries only two. ABO has **six genotypes** and **four phenotypes**: IᴬIᴬ and Iᴬi (A), IᴮIᴮ and Iᴮi (B), IᴬIᴮ (AB), ii (O).

key_terms.definition_md: The heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype.
Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote.

sections.heading: 4. Polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy
sections.body_md:
**Polygenic inheritance.** Traits controlled by **three or more genes**, each adding a small effect, show continuous variation, and the phenotype also reflects the environment. **Human skin colour** is controlled by three genes (A, B, C): AABBCC is the darkest, aabbcc the lightest, and AaBbCc an intermediate shade; the number of dominant alleles decides the colour. With k additive genes, the F2 of two heterozygotes shows **2k + 1 classes**; for three genes, 7 classes, with 1/64 as dark as AABBCC.

**Pleiotropy.** A single gene exhibits **multiple phenotypic expressions**, usually because it affects a metabolic pathway that contributes to several phenotypes.
- **Phenylketonuria (PKU)** in humans: a single-gene mutation in the gene coding for **phenylalanine hydroxylase** manifests as mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.
- **Starch synthesis in pea:** gene B. **BB** plants produce large starch grains and **round** seeds; **bb** plants have less efficient starch synthesis, small grains and **wrinkled** seeds; **Bb** plants have **round** seeds but **intermediate** grain size. So for seed shape B is dominant, but for grain size it shows incomplete dominance — dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene but depends on the phenotype considered.

key_terms.definition_md: Inheritance of a character controlled by several genes with additive effects.

sections.heading: 5. Pedigree analysis
sections.body_md:
Controlled crosses are not possible in humans, so the inheritance of a trait is studied through a family tree, a **pedigree**, over several generations, using standard **symbols**: square (male), circle (female), filled symbol (affected), circle with a dot (carrier female), horizontal line (mating), double line (consanguineous mating), vertical line to offspring, and Roman numerals for generations.

**Clues to the pattern:**
- **Autosomal dominant:** appears in **every generation**; every affected person has at least one **affected parent**; both sexes affected about equally (e.g. myotonic dystrophy).
- **Autosomal recessive:** may **skip generations**; affected children can be born to **two unaffected (carrier) parents**, often in **consanguineous** marriages; both sexes affected (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia, phenylketonuria).
- **X-linked recessive:** mostly **males** affected; passed from **carrier mothers** to sons; an affected father passes the allele to all his daughters (carriers) but to none of his sons (e.g. haemophilia, colour blindness).

Pedigree analysis is the basis of **genetic counselling**, predicting the risk of a disorder in future children.

key_terms.definition_md: A family tree showing the inheritance of a trait over generations.
A heterozygous individual who carries a recessive allele without showing the trait.
Mating between close relatives, shown by a double line.

sections.heading: 6. Chromosomal theory of inheritance, linkage and crossing over
sections.body_md:
Mendel’s work was rediscovered in **1900** by de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak. **Walter Sutton and Theodor Boveri** noted that chromosomes behave like Mendel’s factors: they occur in pairs, segregate at meiosis and assort independently. They united chromosome movement with Mendel’s principles as the **chromosomal theory of inheritance**: genes are located on chromosomes.

**Thomas Hunt Morgan** tested it with the fruit fly ***Drosophila melanogaster*** — easy to grow on simple medium, short life cycle (about two weeks), many progeny from one mating, clear distinction of sexes, and many hereditary variations visible under a low-power microscope.

**Linkage.** In dihybrid crosses of genes on the **X chromosome**, Morgan found that the proportion of parental combinations was much higher than non-parental. He attributed this to the **physical association of genes on a chromosome (linkage)**; **recombination** describes the generation of non-parental combinations, which arises by **crossing over** between homologous chromosomes during meiosis. Some genes were **tightly linked** (low recombination, e.g. 1.3 percent) and others **loosely linked** (higher recombination, e.g. 37.2 percent).

**Gene mapping.** **Alfred Sturtevant**, Morgan’s student, used the **frequency of recombination** between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the **distance** between them and mapped their positions on the chromosome.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving only the phenotypic ratio for a monohybrid F2 (also give 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes).
- Calling incomplete dominance "blending" (the parental types reappear).
- Writing ABO genotypes as AA or AO without the gene symbol I.
- Confusing polygenic inheritance (many genes, one trait) with pleiotropy (one gene, many traits).
- Identifying a pedigree pattern without stating the clue.
- Saying tightly linked genes have high recombination frequency (it is low).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, a ratio, a law, an example, an expected number.
- 2–3-mark questions: Punnett squares with gametes; test crosses; ABO crosses; pedigree interpretation.
- 5-mark questions in parts: dihybrid cross with independent assortment; deviations from Mendelism; linkage with recombination frequency; pedigree analysis with a Punnett square for probability.

questions.stem_md: Homologous chromosomes are best described as

options.text_md: two identical copies of a chromosome joined at the centromere
any two chromosomes of the same size
a pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the same genes at the same loci

questions.solution_md: Homologues are inherited one from each parent and carry the same genes in the same positions — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these was NOT one of the seven pairs of contrasting characters studied by Mendel in pea?
questions.solution_md: Mendel’s seven pairs were stem height, flower colour, flower position, pod shape, pod colour, seed shape and seed colour — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gardener self-pollinates a pea plant for several generations, and every generation shows only white flowers. The plant belongs to a

options.text_md: heterozygous line that will soon produce violet flowers
true-breeding line, homozygous for the flower-colour gene

questions.solution_md: Stable inheritance over many generations of selfing shows a true-breeding (homozygous) line — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Pea plants are easy to use for producing true-breeding lines.

answer.model_answer_md: Pea flowers are naturally **self-pollinating**, so continued selfing gives **homozygous, true-breeding** lines.

questions.solution_md: Self-pollination.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between (i) genotype and phenotype, and (ii) homozygous and heterozygous, using the pea height gene as the example.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Genotype** is the genetic make-up, e.g. **TT, Tt, tt**; **phenotype** is the observable character, e.g. **tall** or **dwarf**. (ii) A **homozygous** plant has **identical alleles** (TT or tt); a **heterozygous** plant has **different alleles** (Tt) and is tall because T is dominant.

questions.solution_md: Two distinctions with examples.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why Mendel succeeded where earlier workers on heredity had failed.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. He chose the **garden pea**: easy to grow, short life cycle, naturally **self-pollinating** with **true-breeding lines**, and easy to cross artificially.
2. He studied **one or two clear contrasting characters** at a time.
3. He used **large samples**, kept careful records and applied **statistics** to his counts. (Also, his characters happened to assort independently.)

questions.solution_md: Three reasons.

marking_scheme.step: One or two characters at a time

questions.stem_md: What phenotypic ratio is expected when a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is test-crossed?
questions.solution_md: Tt × tt gives Tt and tt in equal numbers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a cross between true-breeding tall and dwarf pea plants, all F1 plants are tall. Which principle explains this?
questions.solution_md: Only the dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygous F1 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A true-breeding violet-flowered pea (VV) is crossed with a white-flowered pea (vv). What is the genotype of every F1 plant?

options.text_md: VV and vv in equal numbers

questions.solution_md: Each F1 receives V from one parent and v from the other — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A cross between an F1 hybrid and one of its parents is called a
questions.solution_md: A cross of the F1 with either parent is a back cross; with the recessive parent it is also a test cross — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In the F2 of a dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy, what fraction of plants have wrinkled green seeds (rryy)?
questions.solution_md: Only the ry gamete from each parent gives rryy: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the F2 of a cross between round yellow (RRYY) and wrinkled green (rryy) peas, which phenotypes are new combinations not seen in either parent?
questions.solution_md: Round green and wrinkled yellow appear because the two genes assort independently — option (c).

questions.stem_md: How many genetically different kinds of gametes does a pea plant of genotype RrYy produce?
questions.solution_md: Each gene contributes 2 alleles: $2 \times 2 = 4$ kinds (RY, Ry, rY, ry).

questions.stem_md: How many kinds of gametes can a plant heterozygous for three unlinked genes (AaBbCc) produce?
questions.solution_md: $2^3 = 8$ kinds of gametes.

questions.stem_md: An F2 from a cross of tall (Tt) × tall (Tt) pea plants contains 800 plants. How many are expected to be dwarf?
questions.solution_md: Dwarf (tt) $= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 800 = 200$.

questions.stem_md: A dihybrid F2 (RrYy × RrYy) contains 1600 seeds. How many round green seeds are expected?
questions.solution_md: Round green $= \dfrac{3}{16} \times 1600 = 300$.

questions.stem_md: Among the tall plants of a monohybrid F2 (Tt × Tt), what fraction is heterozygous? Give your answer to two decimal places.
questions.solution_md: Tall plants are TT (1) and Tt (2) out of 3: $\dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When violet-flowered (VV) and white-flowered (vv) pea plants are crossed and the violet F1 is selfed, about one-quarter of the F2 plants bear white flowers.

**Reason (R):** Each Vv plant forms gametes carrying either V or v in equal numbers, because the two alleles separate during gamete formation without blending.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; equal V and v gametes from each F1 parent give vv in one-quarter of the F2, so segregation explains the white flowers — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A violet-flowered pea plant may be VV or Vv. Describe how a test cross can reveal its genotype, giving the expected results.

answer.model_answer_md: Cross it with a **white-flowered (vv)** plant. If **all offspring are violet**, the plant is **VV**; if violet and white appear in a **1 : 1** ratio, it is **Vv**, because it passed on v to half its gametes.

questions.solution_md: Cross with recessive; two outcomes.

questions.stem_md: State the law of independent assortment and explain how a dihybrid F1 obeys it.

answer.model_answer_md: When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the **segregation of one pair is independent of the other**. An RrYy F1 therefore forms **four kinds of gametes** — **RY, Ry, rY, ry** — in **equal** proportions, giving the **9 : 3 : 3 : 1** F2 ratio.

questions.solution_md: Statement; four gametes.

questions.stem_md: Using a Punnett square, work out the F2 phenotypic and genotypic ratios of a cross between true-breeding tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants.

answer.model_answer_md:
**P:** TT × tt → gametes **T** and **t** → **F1 Tt** (all tall).

**F1 × F1:** Tt × Tt; gametes **T, t** from each.

**Punnett square:** TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

Phenotypes: **tall : dwarf = 3 : 1**; genotypes: **TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1**.

questions.solution_md: F1 then F2 with both ratios.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the dihybrid F2 ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 can be obtained by multiplying two monohybrid ratios. What does this show about the two genes?

answer.model_answer_md: Considered separately, seed shape gives **3 round : 1 wrinkled** and seed colour **3 yellow : 1 green** in the F2. If the genes are inherited **independently**, the probability of each combination is the **product** of the separate probabilities: (3 : 1) × (3 : 1) = **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**. This shows that the two genes **assort independently**, as they lie on **different chromosomes** (or far apart).

questions.solution_md: Product rule; independent assortment.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Pure-breeding pea plants with round yellow seeds (RRYY) are crossed with plants with wrinkled green seeds (rryy). Show the F1 and the gametes it forms. [2]
(b) Work out the F2 phenotypic ratio and state the law it illustrates. [2]
(c) How would you confirm that an F2 round yellow plant is RrYy? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) P: RRYY × rryy; gametes **RY** and **ry**; **F1 RrYy**, all round yellow. The F1 forms **four** kinds of gametes in equal numbers: **RY, Ry, rY, ry**.

(b) A 4 × 4 Punnett square of these gametes gives **9 : 3 : 3 : 1** — round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green. It illustrates the **law of independent assortment**.

(c) **Test-cross** it with **rryy**: an RrYy plant gives round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow and wrinkled green in **1 : 1 : 1 : 1**.

questions.solution_md: F1 and gametes; F2 ratio and law; test cross.

questions.stem_md: In snapdragon, a cross between true-breeding red-flowered and white-flowered plants gives pink-flowered F1 plants. This is an example of
questions.solution_md: The heterozygote is intermediate because neither allele is completely dominant — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which genotype gives blood group O?
questions.solution_md: Group O has neither Iᴬ nor Iᴮ: genotype ii — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A man of blood group AB marries a woman of blood group O. Which blood groups can their children have?
questions.solution_md: Gametes Iᴬ or Iᴮ from the father and i from the mother give Iᴬi (A) or Iᴮi (B) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why is blood group AB an example of codominance?

options.text_md: Both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are fully expressed in the same person.
The person shows an intermediate sugar between A and B.

questions.solution_md: In IᴬIᴮ both alleles produce their sugars: codominance — option (b).

questions.stem_md: How many different genotypes are possible for the ABO blood group gene in a population?
questions.solution_md: Three alleles give IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi, IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi, IᴬIᴮ and ii — six genotypes — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A snapdragon F2 from pink × pink (Rr × Rr) has 400 plants. How many are expected to be pink?
questions.solution_md: Pink (Rr) $= \dfrac{2}{4} \times 400 = 200$.

questions.stem_md: Parents of genotypes Iᴬi and Iᴮi have a child. What is the probability that the child has blood group O? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: Child must receive i from both: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.25$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In snapdragon, the phenotypic ratio of the F2 is the same as its genotypic ratio.

**Reason (R):** Snapdragon is commonly called the dog flower.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the common name does not explain the ratio, which follows from incomplete dominance — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Blood group AB is an example of codominance.

**Reason (R):** Alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are both recessive to allele i.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant over i — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: The pink F1 of snapdragon does not prove that the parental alleles have blended.

answer.model_answer_md: Red and white flowers **reappear unchanged** in the F2, so the alleles stayed separate.

questions.solution_md: Parental types reappear.

marking_scheme.step: Red and white reappear in F2

questions.stem_md: A child of blood group O is born to a mother of group A. Could a man of group AB be the father? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: **No.** A group O child is **ii** and must receive **i from each parent**. A man of group **AB (IᴬIᴮ)** has **no i allele**, so he can pass on only Iᴬ or Iᴮ and cannot be the father.

questions.solution_md: AB father cannot give i.

marking_scheme.step: Child ii needs i from each parent

questions.stem_md: Using a Punnett square, explain the F2 of a cross between true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragons. How does it differ from Mendel’s monohybrid result?

answer.model_answer_md:
P: RR × rr → F1 **Rr (pink)**. F1 × F1: Rr × Rr; gametes R, r from each. F2: **RR (red) : Rr (pink) : rr (white) = 1 : 2 : 1**.

In Mendel’s tall × dwarf cross the F2 phenotypic ratio was **3 : 1**, because T is completely dominant. Here the heterozygote is **intermediate**, so the **phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio 1 : 2 : 1**.

questions.solution_md: Cross; comparison.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between incomplete dominance and codominance, with one example of each. [2]
(b) A woman of blood group A whose father was group O marries a man of group B whose mother was group O. Work out the possible blood groups of their children and their probabilities. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In **incomplete dominance** the heterozygote shows an **intermediate** phenotype, e.g. **pink** snapdragon (Rr) from red and white. In **codominance** **both alleles are fully expressed** in the heterozygote, e.g. blood group **AB** (IᴬIᴮ).

(b) The woman received i from her group O father, so she is **Iᴬi**; the man received i from his group O mother, so he is **Iᴮi**. Gametes: Iᴬ, i and Iᴮ, i. Children: **IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O)**, each with probability **0.25** (1 : 1 : 1 : 1).

questions.solution_md: Distinction; cross with probabilities.

questions.stem_md: Human skin colour shows a continuous range of shades. This is because it is

options.text_md: controlled by several genes with additive effects (polygenic)
controlled by one gene with two codominant alleles
a pleiotropic effect of one gene

questions.solution_md: Skin colour is polygenic: each dominant allele adds a small amount of pigment — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A single mutation in the gene for phenylalanine hydroxylase causes both mental retardation and reduced pigmentation of hair and skin. This illustrates
questions.solution_md: One gene with several phenotypic effects is pleiotropic — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In pea, BB plants have round seeds with large starch grains, bb plants wrinkled seeds with small grains, and Bb plants round seeds with intermediate grains. What does this show?

options.text_md: Starch grain size is controlled by the environment only.
Whether an allele seems dominant depends on which phenotype is considered.

questions.solution_md: For seed shape B is dominant, but for grain size Bb is intermediate — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A character is controlled by two additive genes. How many phenotypic classes are expected in the F2 of AaBb × AaBb?
questions.solution_md: Number of dominant alleles 0 to 4: $2k + 1 = 2 \times 2 + 1 = 5$ classes.

questions.stem_md: For a character controlled by two additive genes, what fraction of the F2 of AaBb × AaBb is expected to be AABB? Give a decimal.
Distinguish between polygenic inheritance and pleiotropy, with one human example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In **polygenic inheritance**, **several genes** with additive effects control **one character**, giving continuous variation, e.g. **skin colour**. questions.stem_md: What are linkage and recombination? Explain why linked genes sometimes separate, and how the frequency of their separation relates to distance.

answer.model_answer_md: **Linkage** is the **physical association of genes on the same chromosome**, so they tend to be inherited together. **Recombination** is the generation of **non-parental combinations**. Linked genes separate when **crossing over** exchanges segments between **homologous chromosomes** during meiosis. The **farther apart** two genes are, the more often a crossover falls between them, so **recombination frequency increases with distance** (tightly linked genes show low frequency).

questions.solution_md: Definitions; crossing over; distance.

questions.stem_md: Recombination frequencies between four linked genes are: K–L 8 percent, L–M 3 percent, K–M 11 percent, M–N 6 percent, L–N 9 percent. Work out the order of the genes and explain your reasoning.

answer.model_answer_md: Since **K–M (11) = K–L (8) + L–M (3)**, **L lies between K and M**: K – L – M. Since **L–N (9) = L–M (3) + M–N (6)**, **M lies between L and N**: L – M – N. The order is therefore **K – L – M – N**, with recombination frequency used as a measure of **distance**, as in Sturtevant’s mapping.

questions.solution_md: Additive distances give K L M N.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain how Morgan’s dihybrid crosses in Drosophila showed that some genes do not assort independently. [2]
(b) In a test cross of a fly heterozygous for two linked genes, 1000 offspring include 880 of the two parental types and 120 recombinants. Calculate the recombination frequency and state what it indicates. [2]
(c) Who first used such values to map genes? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Morgan crossed flies differing in two genes on the **X chromosome**. The **parental combinations** appeared **far more often** than the **non-parental (recombinant)** ones, instead of in the equal proportions expected under independent assortment. He concluded that the genes are **physically linked** on the same chromosome and that recombinants arise by **crossing over**.

(b) Recombination frequency $= \dfrac{120}{1000} \times 100 = 12$ percent. It is well below 50 percent, so the genes are **linked**, fairly **close together**.

(c) **Alfred Sturtevant**, Morgan’s student.

questions.solution_md: Morgan’s finding; frequency; Sturtevant.

questions.passage_md:
A student repeated a classic pea experiment. She crossed pure round yellow plants with pure wrinkled green plants, selfed the F1 and counted the F2 seeds.

| F2 phenotype | Count |
|---|---|
| Round yellow | 315 |
| Round green | 108 |
| Wrinkled yellow | 101 |
| Wrinkled green | 32 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 312.8

**(b)** (a) 3 : 1

**(c)** (i) The counts are close to **9 : 3 : 3 : 1**, and each character alone gives about **3 : 1**. So the two genes **segregate** normally and **assort independently**, as stated in Mendel’s **law of independent assortment**.

**OR** (ii) **Round green** and **wrinkled yellow** are new combinations. They appear because the genes for shape and colour **assort independently** during gamete formation, so the F1 forms Ry and rY gametes as well as the parental RY and ry.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Total $= 556$; $\dfrac{9}{16} \times 556 = 312.8$.

**(b)** Round $= 315 + 108 = 423$; wrinkled $= 101 + 32 = 133$; about 3 : 1 — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Independent assortment.

(ii) New combinations from independent assortment.

questions.passage_md:
A hospital recorded the blood groups in one family.

| Person | Blood group |
|---|---|
| Grandfather (mother’s father) | O |
| Mother | A |
| Father | B |
| First child | O |
| Second child | AB |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) Iᴬi

**(b)** (c) Iᴮi

**(c)** (i) The mother can pass on **Iᴬ** and the father **Iᴮ**. The child is **IᴬIᴮ**, and since Iᴬ and Iᴮ are **codominant**, both are expressed, giving group **AB**.

**OR** (ii) Iᴬi × Iᴮi gives IᴬIᴮ, Iᴬi, Iᴮi and ii equally; only **Iᴬi** is group A, so the probability is **0.25** (one in four), whatever the earlier children were.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** She is group A and received i from her group O father — option (b).

**(b)** A group O child (ii) needs i from the father, who is group B — option (c).

**(c)** (i) Iᴬ from mother, Iᴮ from father; codominance.

(ii) One quarter.
